chunks: A bequest [in a will] is not valid except up to one third [of the estate]. Whoever bequeaths more than one third, it is reduced to one third.
A Muslim should bequeath something from his wealth — large or small — to relatives who do not inherit from him. Whoever does not do so has sealed his deeds with a sin.
The shares of inheritance do not exceed six [sixths]. No one inherits together with a child and both parents except a spouse (husband or wife).
A Muslim can inherit from a disbeliever, but a disbeliever cannot inherit from a Muslim.

The son born of li'an does not inherit from his father, nor from anyone on the father's side; his mother inherits from him. If he has no mother, then his maternal uncles and relatives from his mother's side [inherit].

Whenever the li'an husband acknowledges the child after the li'an, the child is affiliated to him but his wife does not return to him. If the father dies, the son inherits from him; but if the son dies, the father does not inherit from him.

key_terms.ابن الملاعنة: Son of li'an — a child disavowed through the li'an procedure; his paternity from the father's side is severed
key_terms.الثلث: One-third — the maximum share that can be bequeathed beyond the fixed inheritance shares
key_terms.الملاعنة: Li'an — a formal mutual oath of imprecation between spouses over an allegation of adultery, which dissolves the marriage and affects paternity
key_terms.الوصية: Bequest/will — a testamentary disposition of property, limited to one-third of the estate in Islamic law
key_terms.تعول: 'Awl — the increase of denominator when shares exceed the estate; this hadith says it does not happen in Shia law
key_terms.سهام المواريث: The shares of inheritance — the fixed fractional portions assigned to heirs in Quranic law

ai.seo_question: What are the Islamic rules for bequests, inheritance shares, and the son of li'an according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from the assembly of Shaykh al-Saduq sets out core Shia inheritance (mawarith) and bequest (wasiyya) rulings. It establishes the one-third limit on testamentary bequests, the moral duty to make charitable bequests to non-inheriting relatives, the principle that inheritance shares do not 'awl (increase beyond the fixed fractions), and special rulings on interfaith inheritance and the li'an (mutual oath of imprecation) scenario. These rulings are grounded in Quranic inheritance verses (4:11-12) and Imami jurisprudence.

en.bilal-muhammad: Bequeathal [in a will] does not exceed one third. Whoever bequeaths more than one third, it is returned to one third.

A Muslim [in such a situation] should bequeath something of his wealth – small or large in sum – to his relatives who do not normally inherit anything from him. Whoever does not do that has sealed his actions [in this world] with a sin.
A Muslim can inherit from a disbeliever, but a disbeliever cannot inherit from a Muslim.

The son of a mala`ina does not inherit from his father, nor from anyone from his father’s side; he inherits from his mother. If he does not have a mother, then from his maternal uncles and his relatives from his mother’s side.
If the father acknowledges the son and the mother does not return to him, then the son inherits from the father, but the father does not inherit from the son.
